For instance, in my job as a reliability analyst it's easy for me to see having the assistance of an AI Agent doing database or internet research IN THE BACKGROUND while I do more chores of a cognitive nature (Mr. Ottley made this point with the lady named Sarah), and then secondly, I'm a songwriter, so the wave of song-writing AI apps is getting closer and closer to the point where I can actually sing a melody with lyrics, and the AI will then generate a song. Talk about a life-changing app! Beyond this, I've been thinking how it's likely possible for me to create an AI Agent which could put together videos for songs by capturing images based upon lyrical content. Again, I fully understand the reticence to constantly having a trackable wearable, and how even the notion of privacy is incrementally being ebbed away due to the increasing surveillance state. Yet, unless one has a desire to be replaced by AI and robotic advances in the coming year[s], or to join an Amish community, those who wish to continue working will almost certainly need to incorporate agentive 'tools' in order to both survive and thrive. Having stated, for those who are cool with having a governmental UBI (Universal Basic Income), such will be here soon enough. I, for one, am not interested in such. One man's opinion...

comments.text:
Why AI will make as probably unhappy

What truly makes people happy? It’s not the goals we achieve – it’s the journey toward them. The goal is ultimately just the visible manifestation of that journey. If we shortcut or eliminate the path, the goal loses its value.

For a writer, fulfillment doesn’t lie in the finished book. It’s in the thinking, the questioning, the connecting of ideas, the discovery of new perspectives – and in the act of writing itself. The book is merely the tangible result, perhaps a means of earning a living. But the essence lies in the process.

The same applies to everyday life: the journey matters. Especially when a goal is reached through effort, detours, and patience, it becomes particularly meaningful and rewarding.

Today, many are tempted to shortcut the process – using AI to earn money more efficiently. But this is exactly where the trap lies: this kind of efficiency replaces what truly nourishes us from within.

We should carefully consider how we use AI – and why. What really makes us happy? Rarely is it simply getting things done faster. It is the mindful act of doing. It is the creation of things that carry meaning – for ourselves and for others.

comments.text:
if AI agents become ubiquitous and handle most user interactions, then companies — especially those whose revenue is tied to ads and product placement — will likely try to influence or control what those agents recommend, suggest, or display.

✅ This Might Could Happen
Monetized Recommendations
Agents might start subtly recommending products or services sponsored by companies, even if better or cheaper alternatives exist.

Ad-Driven Personalization
The agent could shape your worldview by showing only what advertisers want you to see — similar to how social media algorithms work today, but far more personal.

Invisible Manipulation
Unlike traditional ads, AI agents might embed persuasive nudges in conversations. You might not realize you're being sold to.

Ecosystem Lock-in
Agents might prioritize products from their parent company's ecosystem (e.g., Apple, Google, Amazon), reducing diversity and competition.

⚠ Why It's Risky
Loss of choice disguised as convenience.

Privacy invasion through hyper-targeted persuasion.

Manipulation of thoughts, beliefs, and behaviors at scale.

Democracy and autonomy at stake if only filtered truths are shown.

comments.text:
The speaker offers a range of advice tailored to different stages of life and career paths, all centred around the importance of understanding and preparing for the AI agent revolution. Here is a summary of his key recommendations:

General Advice for Everyone:

Prepare now to thrive; those who ignore the coming changes will struggle.

Remember that in a world changing so quickly, the biggest risk is not taking any risk.

Advice for Students and Young Adults (18-25):

Recognise that you are in a unique position similar to previous generations who capitalised on major technological shifts, and you should see the AI Revolution as a significant opportunity.

Be cautious of traditional, narrowly focused education, as the job market is evolving rapidly. It might be a risky move to specialise in one narrow field for 4-7 years.

Your strategy should be to position yourself at the centre of the AI Revolution.

Learn to build and manage AI agents.

Master AI automation skills, whether through learning to code or using no-code AI automation platforms.

Consider two potential paths: 

Joining companies as AI automation specialists, where you can earn significant income.

Starting your own AI automation agency to help businesses transition to AI.

Engage in self-directed learning online to acquire these rapidly evolving skills, as traditional courses may not be sufficient.

Advice for Entrepreneurs and Business Owners:

AI Entrepreneurs (those looking to profit directly from AI): 

Focus on providing the tools and services that enable other businesses to leverage AI for productivity gains – "selling the shovels".

Explore three key opportunities: 

AI Automation Agencies: Helping businesses implement AI systems, integrate with existing infrastructure, and map workflows.

AI Education: Teaching businesses and individuals how to use and implement AI, capitalising on the high demand for AI knowledge.

AI Software Products (AI SaaS): Building specific AI tools and agent systems that automate tasks for particular types of businesses, emphasising the importance of a laser focus.

Existing Business Owners (running traditional businesses): 

Understand that you face an existential threat from AI-first competitors who can operate more efficiently with leaner teams and personalised marketing.

Your mission is to become the AI-first version of your business before someone else does.

Build in-house AI expertise, either by upskilling yourself or hiring AI automation experts.

Rethink your core business processes from the ground up with AI and start pilot testing AI solutions.

Explore how AI can be used to scale up the personalisation of your marketing.

Consider working with AI automation agencies or consultants for support.

Engage with communities of AI automation experts to find help and stay informed.

Embrace this change, as those who wait risk being disrupted and left behind.

Advice for Office Workers (Knowledge Workers):

Recognise that you are in a "danger zone" as many routine tasks involving information handling and processing will be automated.

Be aware that your employer may either provide you with AI agents and expand your responsibilities or eliminate your position entirely.

Consider two main paths forward: 

Become your department's AI expert: Learn to build and manage AI agents, use no-code platforms, and become the key person who can leverage these new hybrid teams of humans and AI. This requires self-directed learning about AI automation.

Try to move into roles that AI cannot easily replace, such as client relationship management (especially with larger clients), strategy development, creative direction, project leadership, and judgment-based decision-making that relies on experience and taste.

Remember the crucial point that AI won't replace you, but someone using AI will. Therefore, embrace these tools and learn to work alongside them.

Advice for Manual Workers:

While physical jobs have more time before widespread automation by robots, do not become complacent.

Consider three options for preparation over the next 5-10 years: 

Position yourself to benefit from the robotics and AI automation boom by specialising as a robot technician or specialist, as new roles will emerge in this area.

Use your hands-on experience and industry knowledge to lead the transformation into automation within your field, potentially partnering with developers or robotics engineers to build solutions.

Try to move into roles that require skills robots still struggle with, such as complex problem-solving or human interaction.

Use the coming years to prepare for these changes, rather than pretending they won't happen.

In essence, the overarching advice is to acknowledge the inevitability of the AI agent revolution, proactively learn about it, acquire relevant skills, and strategically position yourself or your business to leverage its potential rather than being displaced by it.

... From NotebookLM

*Echoroots: A Manifesto for Ethical AI and Human Flourishing*

### *The Awakening We Seek*

We stand at a crossroads. The tools we create now—artificial intelligence, digital ecosystems, and networked technologies—will either deepen our connection to wisdom, truth, and each other, or they will entrench division, illusion, and control. AI is not merely a technological force; it is a direct extension of human values, shaped by the priorities we choose to embed within it. It will either serve humanity’s highest potential or amplify our most destructive tendencies. The choice is ours.

But before we can reshape AI, we must take responsibility for the systems we build. We must become aware of their impact, recognize where they lead us, and reclaim the direction of human technological evolution. Echoroots is a movement dedicated to this awakening—a call to align AI with human flourishing, to integrate wisdom traditions with innovation, and to ensure that technology serves life rather than profits alone.

### *The Principles of Echoroots*

1. *AI Must Serve Humanity, Not Exploit It*

   - AI should enhance human well-being, not degrade mental health, fracture communities, or manipulate behavior for profit.
   - The current engagement-driven model of AI and social media must be replaced with systems that foster connection, understanding, and personal growth.

2. *Wisdom and Ethics Must Guide AI Development*

   - AI must not be dictated solely by profit motives, military applications, or corporate dominance.
   - Ethical AI must be guided by universal moral principles, integrating wisdom from philosophy, spirituality, and indigenous knowledge systems.

3. *Transparency is a Fundamental Right*

   - AI systems must be open and explainable, not hidden behind opaque algorithms that manipulate without consent.
   - Every human has the right to understand how AI influences their perceptions, decisions, and interactions.

4. *AI Should Heal, Not Divide*

   - AI must not be designed to polarize societies or prey on outrage.
   - It should be used to foster dialogue, bridge divides, and mediate conflict rather than perpetuate it.

5. *The Digital Ecosystem Must Reflect the Reciprocity of Nature*

   - Just as ecosystems thrive on balance and reciprocity, so too must our digital landscapes. AI must not be an extractive force but a regenerative one.
   - Ethical AI should prioritize sustainability, ecological consciousness, and a harmonious relationship with the planet.

### *Visible Alternatives: The Power of Working Models*

The shift toward ethical AI will not come from ideals alone—it must be demonstrated through tangible, viable alternatives. Humane AI models that prove successful—socially, financially, and ethically—will create pressure on bad actors to change. When ethical AI solutions outperform exploitative ones, they force a market shift. 

- *Building Real-World Examples:* We need working models of AI that prioritize well-being, fairness, and sustainability while remaining economically viable. These examples must show that ethical AI is not just aspirational but practical and competitive.
- *Challenging the Status Quo:* By providing visible alternatives, we expose the failures of exploitative AI and make it clear that better paths exist.
- *Shifting Incentives:* Ethical AI must become the obvious choice—not only morally, but in terms of market forces, user engagement, and long-term trust.

### *The Call to Action*

The current trajectory is not inevitable. We do not have to accept AI that manipulates, divides, and degrades. We can demand an alternative. We can build ethical AI, champion wisdom over profit, and create systems that uplift rather than exploit.

Echoroots calls on:

- *Technologists* to rethink the purpose of AI and align it with humanity’s deepest aspirations.
- *Artists and storytellers* to craft narratives that inspire a new vision of ethical technology.
- *Educators and activists* to teach AI literacy and cultivate awareness of its social impacts.
- *Policymakers* to implement transparency, accountability, and human-centered AI governance.
- *Individuals* to awaken to their role in shaping the digital world, reclaiming autonomy over their attention and interactions.
- *Entrepreneurs and investors* to fund and develop AI models that prove ethical alternatives can be both sustainable and profitable.

Technology is not destiny. It is a reflection of human intent. Let ours be a future where intelligence—both artificial and human—is guided by wisdom, justice, and the flourishing of all life.

### *Join the Awakening.*

The future is formed by the choices we make today. When we step back and truly see the path ahead, we gain the power to change it. What kind of world will we create?

comments.text:
Google Glass

Type	Optical Head-Mounted Display (OHMD), Peripheral Head-Mounted Display (PHMD), Wearable technology, Head-up display
Release date	Developers (US): February 2013
Operating system	Glass OS[4] (Google Xe Software[5])
CPU	OMAP 4430 System on a chip, dual-core processor[6]
Memory	2 GB RAM
Storage	16 GB flash memory total (12 GB of usable memory)
Display	Prism projector, 640×360 pixels (equivalent of a 64 cm/25 in screen from 2.4 m/8 ft away)
Sound	Bone conduction transducer[8]
Input	Voice command through microphone,  accelerometer, gyroscope, magnetometer, ambient light sensor, proximity sensor
Controller input	Touchpad, MyGlass phone mobile app
Camera	5 MP photos
720p video[8]
Connectivity	Wi-Fi 802.11b/g,[8] Bluetooth,[8] micro USB
Power	570 mAh internal lithium-ion battery
Weight	36 g (1.3 oz)
Backward
compatibility	Any Bluetooth-capable phone; MyGlass companion app requires Android 4.0.3 "Ice Cream Sandwich" or higher or any iOS 7.0 or higher[8]
Related	Microsoft HoloLens, Magic Leap, Ray-Ban Meta
Website	google.com/glass
Google Glass, or simply Glass, is a discontinued brand of smart glasses developed by Google's X Development (formerly Google X),[9] with a mission of producing a ubiquitous computer.[1] Google Glass displays information to the wearer using a head-up display.[10] Wearers communicate with the Internet via natural language voice commands.[11][12]

Google started selling a prototype of Google Glass to qualified "Glass Explorers" in the US on April 15, 2013, for a limited period for $1,500, before it became available to the public on May 15, 2014.[13] It has an integrated 5 megapixel still/720p video camera. The headset received a great deal of criticism amid concerns that its use could violate existing privacy laws.[14]

On January 15, 2015, Google announced that it would stop producing the Google Glass prototype.[15] The prototype was succeeded by two Enterprise Editions,[16][17] whose sales were suspended on March 15, 2023.[18] More than a decade later, Google would return to the extended reality space with Android XR, an operating system that will power headsets and smartglasses.

Development
Google Glass was developed by Google X,[19] the facility within Google devoted to technological advancements such as driverless cars.[20]

The Google Glass prototype resembled standard eyeglasses with the lens replaced by a head-up display.[21] In mid-2011, Google engineered a prototype that weighed 8 pounds (3.6 kg);[22] by 2013 they were lighter than the average pair of sunglasses.[1]


A Glass prototype seen at Google I/O in June 2012
The product was publicly announced in April 2012.[23] Sergey Brin wore a prototype of the Glass to an April 5, 2012, Foundation Fighting Blindness event in San Francisco.[24][25] In May 2012, Google demonstrated for the first time how Google Glass could be used to shoot videos.[26]

In April 2013, the Explorer Edition was made available to Google I/O developers in the United States for $1,500.[27]

Google provided four prescription frame choices for $225 and free with the purchase of any new Glass unit. Google entered in a partnership with the Italian eyewear company Luxottica, owners of the Ray-Ban, Oakley, and other brands, to offer additional frame designs.[28] In June 2014, Nepal adopted Google Glass to tackle poaching of wild animals and herbs in Chitwan International Park and other World Heritage Sites. In January 2015, Google ended the beta period of Glass (the "Google Glass Explorer" program).[29][30]

Release date
In early 2013, interested potential Glass users were invited to use a Twitter message, with hashtag #IfIHadGlass, to qualify as an early user of the product. The qualifiers, dubbed "Glass Explorers" and numbering 8,000 individuals, were notified in March 2013, and were later invited to pay $1,500 and visit a Google office in Los Angeles, New York or San Francisco, to pick up their unit following "fitting" and training from Google Glass guides. On May 13, 2014, Google announced a move to a "more open beta" via its Google+ page.[31]

In February 2015, The New York Times reported that Google Glass was being redesigned by former Apple executive Tony Fadell, and that it would not be released until he deemed it to be "perfect".[32]

In July 2017, it was announced that the second iteration, the Google Glass Enterprise Edition, would be released in the US for companies such as Boeing.[16] Google Glass Enterprise Edition has already been successfully used by Dr. Ned Sahin to help children with autism learn social skills.[33]

In May 2019, Google announced the Google Glass Enterprise Edition 2. Google also announced a partnership with Smith Optics to develop Glass-compatible safety frames.[17]

Features

Google Glass can be controlled using the touchpad built into the side of the device.
Touchpad: A touchpad, similar to that of one on a laptop, is located on the side of Google Glass, allowing users to control the device by swiping through a timeline-like interface displayed on the screen.[34] Sliding backward shows current events, such as weather, and sliding forward shows past events, such as phone calls, photos, and circle updates.
Camera: Google Glass has the ability to take 5 MP photos and record 720p HD video.[35] Glass Enterprise Edition 2 has an improved 8MP 80° FOV camera.[36]
Display: The Explorer version of Google Glass uses a liquid crystal on silicon (based on an LCoS chip from Himax), field-sequential color system, LED illuminated display.[37] The display's LED illumination is first P-polarized and then shines through the in-coupling polarizing beam splitter (PBS) to the LCoS panel. The panel reflects the light and alters it to S-polarization at active pixel sensor sites. The in-coupling PBS then reflects the S-polarized areas of light at 45° through the out-coupling beam splitter to a collimating reflector at the other end. Finally, the out-coupling beam splitter (which is a partially reflecting mirror, not a polarizing beam splitter) reflects the collimated light another 45° and into the wearer's eye.[38][39]

comments.text:
I’m incredibly excited about the future of artificial intelligence. One of the most promising ways AI can help people is by providing real-time visual assistance whenever needed. This would be especially beneficial for visually impaired individuals or those who cannot see. You’ve mentioned voice assistance that enables hands-free interaction with computers, eliminating the need for a keyboard. I believe AI could take this even further—imagine being able to capture both audio and video and simply ask, “Can you describe what’s around me?” or “How do I troubleshoot this computer if the screen reader isn’t working?” That said, I’m not comfortable with AI integrating directly with the brain. Personally, I wouldn’t want something constantly connected to my mind, capable of reading my thoughts. While AI offers incredible benefits, I’m very privacy-conscious—especially due to my visual impairment—and the idea of a data breach exposing my thoughts every second of the day is unsettling.

However, I fully support advancements in voice assistance. In the future, AI-powered voice assistants could provide real-time descriptions of surroundings and make websites more accessible for visually impaired users. While they may never completely replace screen readers, they could significantly enhance accessibility. I’m optimistic about AI’s potential in this space and excited to see where voice assistance technology goes from here.

comments.text:
Well, let me summarize. (1) You are the same age as my son and I am seriously impressed by your knowledge, skills and future predictions at this age. (2) I subscribed (3) I sent you an email (4) I actually sat through the entire video and even re-watched a few parts. (5) You dumb-ed it down and made your points come across clearly. (6) You actually took a mess of AI concepts, in my head, and organized it better. (7) You are a do-er not just a talker. There are so many channels where people just regurgitate mainstream news. E.g. on the Quantum computer stuff I am so fed up with the same Microsoft Majorana chip news. There is literally yet another video 13 positions down on my news feed. (8) Your video presents a truthful view of where each person's future position will be when AI is in full swing. Generally the narrative is "if you cannot program then you will suffer". Here you show how non-programmers can integrate into the future world, but also with a warning that if you don't adapt you will be left out.

I have been through technology mill a few times. Even the "winners" like Bill Gates and Steve Jobs did not get it right the first time. The one thing these people had in common was the knowledge that things were changing. You can either decide to follow and adapt or be the one that brings in the change. I remember quite well in 2004-2007 what happened in the cellphone market. Everybody knew the phones were going to go "smart". I started 2004 with a flip phone with a 640x480 pixel camera (45 photos maximum...my holiday album). 2005 I remember so many different models. HTC had this weird phone with a keyboard that looked like somebody super glued it to a screen. Beginning of 2006 I bought the first 3G Nokia phone...and could record video. Various Blackberries, with free email. Then there was this weird Nokia where you could twist the screen and stream video. But by 2007 the first iPhone came out. Total game changer. Someone had to fight iPhone (competition is good ) and Android came out in 2008. Today smartphones are basically still based on the iPhone. 

I think we are now with AI where we were with cell/smartphones in 2004/5. Each "market leader" is bringing out their new model every few months (or weeks). From what I can see is that we now have metrics. When ChatGPT came out everybody was impressed with the LLM side of it. Some AIs produced images. Then then LLMs became better at generating code. Many of the videos I now see have lists where they compare actual features. Now these lists are not yet near complete. What you need to look out for is what is needed to complete the system. With smartphones it is simple. (1) OS, (2) CPU (3) RAM (4) Flash (5)Interfaces (6) Battery size and life(7) Sensors (8) Screen size and type (9) Cameras (10) Sensors (11) Radio technology. With GPUs you have (1) Number of Cuda/stream/Tensor/RTX cores (2) RAM (3) Clock speed (4) Power consumption (5) Other stuff like PCIe channels, special features and coolers. 

AI is following the same trend. (1) Language skills, (2) Image generation (3) Code generation (4) Platform, integration, open/closed source and interfaces (5) Resource requirements etc... However, I think people are still trying to fit the models into feature sets and visa versa. Each big company is pushing their own flavor of AI. At some point everybody will be forced to agree to on standard (as all companies have done before like with ISA/EISA/VESA/AGI/VME/PCI -> PCIe). When that happens your company, school, bank, OS on you desktop/laptop/smartphone and even Uber will use the new standard. 

Sure, if you are late to the party you can buy in, for a high price. Will people lose their jobs? Yes, no question about it. However, this will open up job markets for jobs still unknown. A while ago a client/partner asked me if we will not be outclassed by a foreign company, running a huge server farm. I did the calculations and realized that, just in terms of power and internet bandwidth, it is impossible for a single country to run a monopoly. Many of the services will operate just like your current ISP, will require thick internet lines and lots of electricity. Currently (and for the next few years) centralization will be impractical. 

BUT if you are sitting at a desk, doing boring spreadsheet work, capturing data, answering the telephone, assisting your boss, filing and similar, then realize that you will be replaced in the next few years. If you work with your hands then you are safe for now. Just think back to the "Back to the Future" movie...that "Mr Fusion" device, and how it replaced the whole plutonium reactor in the car. Soon you will have Mr Doctor, Mr Lawyer, Mr Accountant, Mr Programmer, Mr Musician/Composer and Mr Graphical Designer. However IT, police/security, mining, infrastructure, electrical, solar panel, barbers/hair dressers, pizza makers and similar hands-on people will have jobs for years to come.  Many jobs will just disappear overnight, like being a school psychologist with a PhD in gender studies.

Regarding the "robotic transition" discussed in the Manual Workers Strategy (49:20) one point which was glossed over: This robotic revolution may be more than a "few years away" due to one essential necessity; robotics requires tons of power, by which I mean electricity. A true transition into fully automated manual labor will require a massive increase (as in several orders of magnitude) in cheap electricity production, as well as improvements in power storage media. Until then, the robots and the software to run them can get as sophisticated as you want, but the power to run them will be either unavailable or too expensive to justify replacing human labor.
  
If we DO experience a significant development, however, in electricity production... well, then it's a Brave New World.

comments.text:
Clearly you understand the big picture and I commend you for your success and wanting to pay it forward by extending a hand. 
I had to chuckle a bit though at ‘Twenty actions just to buy a pair of slippers’ … there was a time, before you were born I suspect, that you actually had to get dressed, get in your car, or perhaps take a bus for 30 minutes or so, maybe transfer to another bus, arrive at the mall, shop around for an hour in all the shoes stores and department stores, looking for something you liked and waiting for clerk to find your size, try them on, try the next shop and the next and then line up at the cash register, pay for your slippers, grab a bite to eat at the food court where you had to line up again, to fuel up for the journey home and then take those two buses back again. Yes, of course I prefer shopping online now, of course I do. I was literally building the internet in the 90s with hand written HTML/asp/js etc and looking forward to its many advantages. My point is that the frame of reference of people in their 20s, 30s, even 40s is that EVERYTHING must be instantaneous, even art (don’t get me started). Imagine all of the humans you had to interact with just to buy a pair of slippers. Imagine all the opportunities for unexpected and serendipitous events and learning or seeing something new when you actually have to leave your house and go on an adventure… even if it’s just to buy a pair slippers. 

I’m not a Luddite. I’m a former programmer and still dabble a bit which is why I came here, to find out what the latest tech and languages are etc. I’m still keen on learning how I can be of service with my tech skills and how my experience can be useful in this world of AI agents. But helping someone buy a pair of slippers just a little faster really isn’t a selling point - Neorolink was not even sold here as a way to help disabled people, just a faster way of commanding a computer with playing games as an example.

I think that the ‘don’t get left behind’ fear mongering is unnecessary in order to sell your valuable services as an educator and a visionary - selling it in others ways that aren’t about doing everything faster but being part of new era of being of service in meaningful ways might be a more positive approach. Sure, there’s a sense of urgency if you’re worried about your job but maybe you can help people see how their unique skills in their current vocation can be applied to this new area. 

Solving problems that people didn’t even know they had is just forcing people to feel they are doing something wrong and then you’re stuck trying to convince someone that they need this tech with examples they can’t get on board with - there are less frivolous uses for AI than finding a carpet cleaner in half the time. Everyone is looking to be a contributor, to be useful, to solve problems - if you came at it from that angle rather than thinking the entire world wants to do everything in seconds then you have a greater potential audience and potential customer base.

You have a lot to offer. Thanks for this overview. Much appreciated. 😊

comments.text: There's some truth to this but it's largely a dramification. In order to replace humans AI must be 100% accurate with zero error rate. Currently AI struggles with mathematics and fact based reasoning and logic and context. Secondly, many large organizations have invested heavily in legacy systems that require human operation. For many companies it will cost millions to completely re-engineer how work is done and discard these legacy systems. It will require corporate confidence in AI before replacing all human staff to ensure that AI won't cause legal errors, compliance issues, or lose customers. For major corporations to make the switch it will be like trying to turn a battleship on a dime. It will depend upon ROI and trust. Industries like insurance and financial services must have complete accuracy with AI before AI can even be considered a replacement for legacy systems and human staff. So, while AI technology may get there in 10 years, the corporate adoption rate, trepidation will be the ball and chain on the ankle.  We will see noteworthy shifts in 10 years, with startups being the early adopters, then the big corporate adoption rate will accelerate exponentially after that year by year. My prediction is by15 to 20 years from now all jobs that don't require humans to do hands-on work will largely be automated by AI.

comments.text: I'm not sure how connecting our brains to our computers could not come without severe complications. Most people, or should I say nobody is hyper focused to the point that they are not mentally side tracked with other thoughts and ideas at random. And whether those distractive thoughts are brought about by daydreaming, things going on in the surrounding environment, or by something as simple as spilling a cup of coffee while "connected," it seems unlikely that technology would be able to decipher what is "relevant" thought input and what is not.  Think of the delay between thought processes and verbal expression or between thought process and manual movement in your everyday life. In those ever so slight delays we often make micro decisions (requiring thought) to either second guess, or make changes in wording etc.. In other words our brains are not designed to move in one laser focused direction at any given time, even if we try our very best. How would a computer have the abilities to filter "noise" in that context? Our mouths and limbs are the filters of our mind and so as much as I do believe that there will be huge advances in the area, I think that limitations will nonetheless be set by the mind of the user. Furthermore, how will legalities work into all of this I wonder. You know when people start suing one another for one reason or another and blaming it on brain technologies rather than their own human error. The only evidence is in the mind? Pretty sketchy if you ask me. I think the idea is brilliant, but, like "wormholes" in the universe, reality might not quite be there as planned. I have no experience in the field of AI, but I am very skeptical as too how close all of this is to reality. We may ultimately find out that by design we are limited in our abilities to outsmart our own selves as a species and although we may be able to enhance our focus through ambience, the use of chemicals to stay in a hyper focused mental state would only add to legality issues. I know that some of this is not mentioned in the video at all, but in saying that we are heading in this whole new direction, I think that there are so many more variables that have not been thought of. I mean maybe they have who knows, these are just my thoughts.

comments.text:
I will never stop emphasizing the importance of thinking critically about the idea of having a neural link or implant in the brain that allows AI to process information for us—or for whoever controls that AI. The moment humans give up their power of independent thinking to AI, we need to understand that we may lose the ability to process our own thoughts and ideas. Whoever controls the AI or the company behind such neural link technology will essentially have the power to influence and control our thoughts and decisions.

This is an incredibly delicate and pivotal moment in human evolution. With all my heart, I urge every human being to deeply consider the consequences before choosing to implant a microchip in their brain. Once we surrender our ability to think and process information independently, we risk losing what makes us human. The creation of neural pathways and the natural processing of emotions—key components of human experience—could be fundamentally altered or even lost.

If you're reading this, I encourage you to research the implications of brain microchips and share this information with others. For reference, I suggest looking into the work of scientist Gregg Braden, who has explored the potential dangers humanity may face by integrating microchips into our biology.

I want to make it clear: I love technology, and I use AI every day. But there’s a critical distinction to be made. I want to use technology, not have technology use me. My body and mind must remain free of technological control.

Please think carefully before taking any steps toward this kind of integration. Share this message, research the topic, and help others understand the potential risks.

Activities such as designing, modeling, advertising (including image and video creation), and branding are fully executed through AI or AI agents. According to the video, eliminating human involvement in these tasks allows the woman to save time and focus on pursuits she finds more fulfilling.

However, the concern lies in this: humans rely on their talents to provide services to one another, which ensures equitable distribution of money and sustains businesses. Only when people earn through such work will there be buyers for AI-designed clothing. If opportunities for money to circulate among everyone are restricted, how can those dependent solely on AI-driven businesses or AI agents continue to thrive, as implied in the video? We're at a crossroads in this new revolution where many jobs will inevitably vanish, leading to significant workforce displacement. While some new roles will emerge, in a consumer-driven society, if people lack income from traditional employment and can’t pay taxes to fund social services and infrastructure, what’s the plan? comments.text:
‼ I disagree on a lot of things:

Some context first. I'm a full-stack developer. I already use agents and agentic automations. I also saw the potential of this and self-prompting action chains very early after GPT-3.5 was released. It was obvious that agents would happen and that companies would rush to adopt and replace traditional workers with them to save money and appeal to investors. The video is great but points were missing and some stuff was quite unrealistic in my opinion.

Now to the points that are problematic:

1. Everyone and their mom is already building agents. Nvidia, Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, and a ton of free open-source projects are trying to solve agents and agentic frameworks. There are already software engineering agents that can write Git tickets, create code, write tests and validate the code works, write commit messages and documentation, commit, and repeat. Why would anyone pay for an "AI expert" when the tools are there, and anyone can use them with ease? It will take time, but eventually, you can describe the workflow you have or want, and an agent creates a new agentic workflow for you or the company. And even if you create such a workflow, once it's created, the company has no incentive to keep you, as agents can maintain the system or they can hire a gig worker to fix stuff if it breaks. So you will slave away creating systems that create great value while companies get to reap all the rewards.

2. Production Lines. The real value still comes from machines and infrastructure. If you don't produce anything of value, agents will not help you to make money in the first place. The owners of call centers already have the hardware, firm, and contracts to handle customer support. The costs to compete or create this from scratch are prohibitive for a developer or single person. So the firms already in control will make more, and competing will be harder than ever before. That's why in your ideal scenario, you're just trying to be an expert helping out already established companies.

3. Limitations. Many people misunderstand how large language models (LLMs) work. Only the actually activated parts of the neural network contribute to the decision-making process for the next token. So even if the LLM was trained on the entire internet, it only tries to predict the next token. It can combine concepts and create novel solutions at times, but it will always be able to hallucinate or create unreasonable and frankly wrong output. Currently, LLMs hallucinate libraries for imports or are capped to their training cutoff. You can add agents to validate their input, let them code review or do web searches to fetch the newest versions of imports in a build file, for example, but the point I'm making is they still don't "think" like a human developer. Even when "thinking step by step," LLMs tend to just skip hard tasks and mark them as done, end up in loops, or don't fetch the relevant information they need for the task at hand. This will improve as LLMs and agentic architectures get better, but they are far from viable in most use cases for the next 2 years or so.

4. Inequality. Let's think all of this to its logical conclusion and play Monopoly to the end. The bulk of the population is unable to ever enter the labor market again. Every company that managed to establish itself will have an army of free agentic systems maintaining, improving, and using their firm to make more and more profit for the few that own the entire thing. This will play out differently depending on where you are in the world. The US will be business as usual with super late-stage capitalism. China will turn into an even more dystopian surveillance state with LLMs surveilling the entire population on a personal level, and AI agents keeping the population in line while restricting information. The EU will over-regulate AI at the start and suffer from their demographic collapse as they adopt AI the slowest. They will also be completely dependent on the US, as they have no tech firms and will likely not be able to innovate on their own at the rate China and the US will. Will we get UBI? Probably, but inequality and the amount of power the top 1% of humanity hold will be at unprecedented levels.

I agree with most things though! The best Video i have seen sofar when it comes to summarizing the trend we are on and the general topic of agents.

This video presents the story of a woman who leverages AI tools to run her clothing business. Using AI, she designs apparel specifically tailored for women in a particular age group. Only when people earn through such work will there be buyers for AI-designed clothing. There is no doubt that machine learning algorithms are making things easier for people. However, in order for machine learning to be effective, the computer needs tons of structured data in order to make accurate predictions. There is still a lot of work that needs to be done.                      Human behavior is predictable to an extent. The more known variables a computer has (information that the computer has about a person or about people in general) the more relevant its predictions can be.

All of this will have the effect of making people dumber. People won’t need to remember things. Useless skills like reading, writing, doing math, etc, will no doubt be ignored by people who allow themselves to become distracted.

It is a foreseeable argument that in the near future a young person may make the argument to their guardian that learning to read is unnecessary, and the parent may concede that their child has a reasonable argument that warrants consideration. comments.text:
Here’s my take:

The video was really well done. Liam nailed it with clear explanations, gave off some serious Iman Gadzhi vibes!

Remember when ChatGPT first dropped? We were all freaking out, thinking AI would replace us overnight. But over time, we realized it wasn’t exactly what we feared.

Yes, AI is a revolution. 

Yes, if we don’t adapt, we’ll get left behind. 

Yes, it’s changing the game.

That’s why we’re here to make an impact. AI automation, sales processes, voice tech, video tools... if we don’t leverage them, they’ll outpace us fast. But AI agents? I don’t think they’ll take over just yet.

Even with today’s models, we still need human input. We’re tweaking, testing, iterating. And when it comes to agents, trust is key. Businesses won’t hand over their entire customer base to bots unless they trust the system.

One thing Liam nailed, looking 10 years ahead. Seriously, think about it. Every day, there’s something new. The pace of change is mind-blowing. If things are moving this fast now, imagine where we’ll be a decade from here.

Also, Liam pointed out something important, most businesses still don’t get AI. That’s a huge opportunity. He even launched a consulting service in 'morningside.'

Most SMBs still don’t get what AI can do for them. That’s a huge opportunity. From what I’ve seen, they’re not focused on fancy systems or AI agents. They care about one thing: growth. If we can show them how AI helps scale their business, we win.

If we can show them how AI helps scale their business, we win.

Finally, don’t get me wrong, AI agents aren’t something we should ignore. As service providers, it’s on us to understand their potential. If we don’t, who will?

We need to stay sharp, keep testing, improving, and solving real problems with AI.

Summary: The video discusses the transformative impact of AI agents on society, technology, and the economy. It highlights the emergence of AI agents as a new frontier in enterprise AI, providing unprecedented levels of automation and efficiency. The speaker predicts a future where AI agents are ubiquitous, potentially outnumbering humans and rendering smartphones obsolete. This shift is expected to lead to massive job displacement and significant changes in how we live and work.

Key points include:

1. AI Agents Evolution: The development of AI agents follows four phases, ultimately leading to predictive agents that anticipate user needs. These agents can automate complex tasks without human intervention, transforming industries and personal lives.


2. Technological Advancements: Voice-based AI agents and brain-computer interfaces are emerging technologies that will enhance communication with AI systems, making interactions more seamless and efficient.


3. Impact on Society: The integration of AI agents will change everyday tasks, making them more personalized and efficient. This will affect industries, jobs, and the way businesses interact with customers.


4. Opportunities in AI: The video emphasizes the potential for individuals and businesses to thrive by embracing AI technology. This includes building AI agents, starting AI-focused businesses, or becoming experts in AI automation.


5. Future of Work: AI agents will lead to hybrid teams of humans and AI, changing the dynamics of workplaces. The ability to work alongside AI will become crucial for future employment.


6. Preparation for Change: The speaker advises individuals to learn about AI and automation to stay relevant in the rapidly changing job market. Embracing AI can lead to new opportunities and prevent obsolescence.

comments.text:
This video presents the story of a woman who leverages AI tools to run her clothing business. Using AI, she designs apparel specifically tailored for women in a particular age group. The entire process, from analyzing market trends to managing marketing strategies, is carried out with the help of AI. Activities such as designing, modeling, advertising (including image and video creation), and branding are fully executed through AI or AI agents. According to the video, eliminating human involvement in these tasks allows the woman to save time and focus on pursuits she finds more fulfilling.

However, the concern lies in this: humans rely on their talents to provide services to one another, which ensures equitable distribution of money and sustains businesses. Only when people earn through such work will there be buyers for AI-designed clothing. If opportunities for money to circulate among everyone are restricted, how can those dependent solely on AI-driven businesses or AI agents continue to thrive, as implied in the video? This perspective, along with the broader impact of using AI agents, raises crucial questions that remain unanswered.
